summary: Proposes NETED, a common context editor with the same user interface on all servers, following surprising agreement on the idea at a resource sharing workshop. It was part of a broader proposal for a unified user-level protocol. The RFC is now historic.

eli5.summary: Every computer had its own way to edit text. The idea was one editor that works the same everywhere, so you only learn it once. It is now historic.

subtitle: Proposal for a unified text editor across all network systems

tldr.problem: Network users had to learn different editor commands on every host system, making it difficult for non-programmers to use the network effectively and slowing down experienced users.
tldr.mechanism: NETED is a simple line-oriented context editor based on Multics's eds program, offering a common user interface across all systems with just 12 basic commands for navigation, search, insert, replace, delete, and change operations.
tldr.outcome: The Network User Interest Group endorsed NETED as a simple, implementable standard. RFC 569 is now Historic, as the proposal did not achieve universal adoption.

today: RFC 569 is a Historic proposal. While NETED was endorsed, it did not achieve universal adoption across the network. Different systems continued using their own editors, and the problem it addresses was eventually addressed differently through graphical interfaces and unified development environments.

sections.title: The Problem of Many Editors
sections.content:
Network users who work with multiple hosts must learn different editor commands for each system, since there were even more editors than operating systems in 1973. TECO and QED were popular on different systems but had strong, mutually exclusive advocates and varying feature sets, making it impractical to choose one of them as a standard. For non-professional programmers coming into the network community, the burden of learning a dozen different editing interfaces was a serious barrier to productivity.

The Resource Sharing Workshop and the Network User Interest Group both recognized that having a single, simple editor available on all servers would greatly improve the user experience, particularly for those who are not experienced programmers and just want to get work done.
sections.eli5: Each system had its own editor with weird commands. Programmers hated learning new ones. Regular people found it overwhelming. Everyone agreed one editor for all systems would be better.

sections.title: NETED: A Simple Line Editor
sections.content:
NETED is based on the eds program from Multics, a line-oriented context editor with no regular expressions but also no line numbers. It is simple enough to learn but powerful enough for practical editing. NETED operates in two modes: input mode (for creating new files or appending text) and edit mode (for altering existing files). The edit mode maintains a conceptual pointer to the current line, and commands move the pointer or modify the current line.

The 12 basic commands are: n (move forward/backward), l (locate string), t (move to top), b (move to bottom), . (enter input mode), i (insert line), r (replace line), p (print), c (change string), d (delete), w (write), and save (write and exit). The RFC emphasizes sticking to the published Multics code rather than adding new features, to keep implementation in man-days rather than man-weeks.
sections.eli5: NETED is a simple editor: move the cursor up or down, find words, add lines, delete lines, change text. It has 12 commands. The whole thing is easy to learn and easy to implement on any computer.

sections.title: Implementation and Endorsement
sections.content:
The RFC was reviewed by the Network User Interest Group and endorsed by them as an important step toward standardizing the user experience. The author, Mike Padlipsky, had already made a version available to anonymous users on Multics. The RFC explicitly notes that NETED is not proposed as "THE" network editor, but as a simple, implementable option for non-professional programmers and a working model that avoids endless feature haggling. The limitations are intentional: the editor keeps its original feature set from the Multics version to ensure compatibility and predictability.

The RFC encourages feedback from system programmers at sites like TENEX, CCN, UCSD, UCSB, AMES-67, and DEC 10/50 hosts, with the ideal outcome being that they adopt NETED and make it available to their users.
sections.eli5: Users and the network team liked the idea. The author put it on the Multics computer so people could try it. The plan was for other computers to implement it too and offer it to their users.

references.text: Multics Programmer's Manual, Chapter 4, Part I, pp. 24-54.
